w: Built between 1864 and 1904, this Anglican cathedral had already survived earthquakes in 1881, 1888, 1901 and 1922 before February 2011 destroyed its spire and upper tower outright. The remaining tower stump was demolished in March 2012, and the rose-window west wall partly collapsed in later aftershocks. Legal battles over demolition versus restoration have left it standing, deconsecrated, ever since.
_facts: Legal battles over demolition vs restoration

w: Japanese architect Shigeru Ban framed this transitional cathedral's walls and roof with more than 90 large cardboard tubes, opening it in August 2013 on the site of the former St John the Baptist Church. Built with Warren and Mahoney as the Anglican Diocese's stand-in pro-cathedral after Christ Church Cathedral's collapse, it stands a few blocks away in Latimer Square.
s: A cathedral framed from 90-plus cardboard tubes
_facts: Designed by Shigeru Ban with Warren and Mahoney
Over 90 cardboard tubes form walls and roof

w: An English oak planted in 1863 to mark the marriage of the Prince of Wales and Princess Alexandra of Denmark began these 21-hectare gardens beside a loop of the Avon River. Alongside Hagley Park, they hold conservatories, a nursery, a working Climatological Station and collections of both exotic and native New Zealand plants.
s: Gardens begun with a royal-wedding oak, 1863
_facts: Includes conservatories and a Climatological Station

w: At 164.637 hectares this is Christchurch's largest urban open space, set aside in 1855 by the Provincial Government and decreed 'reserved forever as a public park.' It takes its name from Lord Lyttelton's English country estate; Lyttelton chaired the Canterbury Association that founded the settlement in 1850.
_facts: 164.637 hectares, the city's largest urban open space
Decreed reserved forever as a public park
Named for Lord Lyttelton's English estate

w: Christchurch's Anglican cathedral stands at the theoretical crossing of Colombo and Worcester Streets, the city's two main axes, though both are now blocked off or detoured around the square itself. Badly damaged in the February 2011 earthquake, the Square remains the geographical and symbolic heart of the city.
_facts: Theoretical crossing of Colombo and Worcester Streets
Both streets now diverted around the square

w: The wooden original opened on 18 January 1894 and stood until its demolition in October 1965; the concrete pier that replaced it opened on 1 November 1997. Extending out over the Pacific from the New Brighton beachfront, it is now counted among Christchurch's defining landmarks.
s: Beachfront pier, rebuilt in concrete in 1997

w: Julius von Haast's personal collection became the founding core of this museum when it opened in 1867 in the city's Cultural Precinct. The building carries a Category I Historic Place listing from Heritage New Zealand, and it remains one of the country's oldest and most significant museum institutions.
s: Founded 1867 on Julius von Haast's own collection
_facts: Founding collection from Julius von Haast

n: Air Force Museum of New Zealand
w: This museum opened on 1 April 1987 at Wigram, the Royal New Zealand Air Force's very first operational base, timed to mark the RNZAF's 50th anniversary. It covers the RNZAF, its predecessor the New Zealand Permanent Air Force, and the New Zealand squadrons that once flew under the Royal Air Force.
s: Air force museum at the RNZAF's first base
_facts: Sited at the RNZAF's first operational base, Wigram
Covers the RNZAF and its NZ Permanent Air Force predecessor

w: This open-air museum in the Heathcote Valley occupies the site of New Zealand's first public railway. Founded in 1964 when a cluster of local heritage groups pooled their need for storage and display space, it was known first as the Museum of Science and Technology, then Ferrymead Historic Park, and still runs largely on volunteer labour.
s: Open-air museum on NZ's first railway site
_facts: Site of New Zealand's first public railway
Formerly the Museum of Science and Technology

w: The Muslim Association of Canterbury, founded in 1977, built this Riccarton mosque between 1983 and 1985. It became the primary site of the 15 March 2019 Christchurch mosque shootings, an attack that shook New Zealand and drew global attention to the city's small, longstanding Muslim community.
s: Riccarton mosque, site of the 2019 attack
_facts: Run by the Muslim Association of Canterbury, founded 1977
Primary site of the 15 March 2019 shootings

w: Kate Sheppard lived in this Ilam villa from 1888 to 1902, the years she led the campaign that won New Zealand women the vote. Later home to the city's 30th mayor, John Joseph Dougall, it carries a Category I heritage listing and was bought by the government in 2019, opening as a suffrage museum the following year.
s: Kate Sheppard's home during the suffrage campaign
_facts: Later home of Mayor John Joseph Dougall
Government-purchased 2019, opened as a museum in 2020

w: These are the only purpose-built provincial government buildings still standing anywhere in New Zealand, raised for the Canterbury Provincial Council that ran the province from 1853 until provincial government was abolished in 1876. The February 2011 earthquake left them substantially damaged, and the city council has since partially demolished what remained.
s: NZ's only surviving provincial government buildings
_facts: Only purpose-built provincial buildings left in NZ

w: Built in 1876 to drop a time ball so ships in the harbour could set their chronometers, this station finally collapsed on 13 June 2011 after a magnitude 6.4 aftershock, having already been battered through the preceding year of earthquakes. The tower was partially rebuilt and reopened in November 2018.
s: A time ball tower felled by the 2011 quakes
_facts: Collapsed 13 June 2011 in a magnitude 6.4 aftershock

w: Locals nicknamed the shattered remains of this sea stack 'Shag Pile,' a carpet pun coined after the February 2011 earthquake broke it apart. Long a navigation marker at the mouth of the Avon Heathcote Estuary near Sumner, it once guided small vessels crossing the Sumner bar; its broken silhouette is still plainly visible from the road.
s: A shattered sea stack locals call 'Shag Pile'
_facts: Marks the entrance to the Avon Heathcote Estuary

w: Part of the crater wall of the extinct volcano that carved out Lyttelton Harbour, this Port Hills summit displays some of the clearest lava flow formations anywhere on the range. Its reserve looks down over both Christchurch and Lyttelton, a cross-section of the volcanic geology beneath the whole city.
s: Crater-rim summit with visible lava flows
_facts: Part of Lyttelton Harbour's ancient crater wall
Reserve shows notable lava flow examples
